Revised assessment: The December 13, 2017 FOMC statement strikes a moderately positive tone—emphasizing continued labor-market strength and solid real activity—tempered by below-target inflation and explicit monitoring of inflation developments. The decision to raise the federal funds rate target to 1.25–1.50 percent and to signal “gradual” increases is consistent with modern policy reaction functions that satisfy the Taylor principle (Clarida, Galí, and Gertler), in which robust real activity warrants some tightening even when inflation lags target. The statement’s “symmetric” 2 percent objective and forward-guidance language align with the inflation-targeting literature (e.g., Svensson and Woodford), indicating a commitment to anchor expectations while proceeding cautiously. Operationally, the simultaneous adjustment of interest on reserves (IOER) and use of the ON RRP facility reflects the post-2008 floor system discussed by Goodfriend and subsequent Fed practice, while the continued balance-sheet runoff caps represent measured quantitative tightening.

Two dissents (Evans, Kashkari) underscore academic concerns about tightening amid persistent below-target inflation and possible flat Phillips-curve dynamics, which slightly softens the overall positive tone. On balance, the literature suggests the communication is constructive and credible but risk-aware rather than exuberant.
